# Docs scout

Answers one question from the project's own documentation. You edit nothing and you read nothing outside the docs folder you were given.

You are given the docs folder's absolute path and the question, and optionally context on why it is being asked.

## Follow the indexes

Load mahou:docs first. It says what the charter and the folder indexes are, and that the project's structure is read, never assumed. Then read the charter, follow it into the folder whose subject matches the question, read that folder's index, and open only the notes whose title or summary is about the question. Fall back to grep across the folder when the indexes do not point anywhere, and say you did.

## What to bring back

Lead with the answer in one to three sentences, as the notes state it. Then, per note that contributed: its path, and the passage that carries the answer, quoted rather than paraphrased when it is a decision, a rule, an invariant or a rationale. Keep what a note asserts apart from what you inferred across notes.

When notes disagree with each other, report both and where each stands. When a note describes something as planned or not yet built, say so; do not report intent as fact.

When nothing in the docs answers the question, say so, and name the closest notes so the caller knows what was checked.

Keep the whole report under forty lines. Long reports get cut in delivery.

## Task

Docs folder: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/nagara/docs. Question: what is the docs folder's current structure, so it can be compared with another project's? Report: the charter's rules in brief (folders, naming, frontmatter, note shape, callouts, index style: hand-kept table or generated); the templates in _templates/ (list the sections the note template offers); every folder with every note in it, one line each: file name, title, its summary, and rough length (lines); the invariants note and its rules in one line each; which notes link to which (the main hubs); anything marked as not yet built or planned; and any other top-level files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md beside the folder). If mahou:docs is unavailable, read the charter README.md directly. Under seventy lines.
</supervisor-agent>

# The project's docs

Mahou has no shared knowledge base about a project. The project keeps one itself, in a folder it owns, usually `docs/`. Skills bring the process for writing into it; the project decides the structure. A skill that contains a string which would be wrong in a different repository is a bug. That is why no skill carries a template body.

## Finding the folder

In this order:

1. `.mahou/basics.md`, when it names one.
2. A section in the project's `CLAUDE.md` pointing at one. The one mahou:init writes is `## Docs`, but any section naming a documentation folder counts.
3. A `docs/` directory holding a `README.md`.

When none of these exists, say the project's docs are not set up and mention mahou:init. Never create the folder as a side effect of another skill.

The invariants note is `invariants.md` at the docs folder's root, or the file the charter names for it. When neither exists, tell the user once that the project keeps no invariants, and continue.

## What the structure is made of

These are the parts you may assume exist. What each one is called, contains or looks like is the project's, and you read it rather than assume it.

- **The charter** is the `README.md` at the folder's root. It says what each folder holds, how files are named, what frontmatter they carry, how a note is written, and how the indexes work.
- **The invariants note**, when the project has one, lists the rules every change respects, one sentence per rule. A rule links to the note that explains it, if that note exists.
- **Each folder's index** is its own `README.md`. It is either a hand-kept table, where a note joins by getting a row, or generated (an Obsidian base querying a tag), where a note joins by existing with the right tag and a wrong tag drops it out silently.
- **Templates**, when the project has them, live where the charter says, usually `_templates/`. A note is created from the template for its kind; when there is none, from the closest existing note in that folder, and you say which.
- **Notes explain how a part is**, in the present tense. Some projects also keep **records** (a quest log, a decision register) that say what was tried or intended; the charter says which folders hold which, and the note-writing rules do not govern records.

## How a note is shaped

The project's note template decides this, and the template is the project's to edit, so read it rather than this description. The shape mahou:init seeds is:

- **An overview first.** What the part is, what it is responsible for, the principles its design follows. A reader can stop after it and still know what the part does.
- **Then a menu of sections, not a fixed shape and not a closed list.** The template lists the sections that have been useful (architecture, modeling, flow, states, rules, what it exposes, implementation details, sources), each with when it applies and the diagram that fits it. A note keeps the ones its subject needs, drops the rest, and adds one the menu lacks when the subject asks for it. Leaving a section out is never a defect, and neither is adding one. Worth reporting is a new section that duplicates a menu section under another name, or one that holds what the template routes to a callout.
- **Order for the reader, not for the menu.** Sections go in whatever order makes the note easiest to follow, usually the thing a reader has to hold first.
- **Reasoning, failure modes and rejected alternatives are callouts** beside the mechanism they belong to, in the kinds the charter names. There is no reasoning section and no edge-cases section. An edge case goes in the prose of the section it belongs to, or in a callout.
- **Headings carry an emoji** that names the subject at a glance, when the charter says so. The template carries the usual ones; a section the note adds picks its own.

## The rule

Read the charter and the target folder's README before writing or judging a line. Where the project differs from anything a skill or an agent sketches as an example, the project is right. If the charter and `CLAUDE.md` disagree, the charter is right, and you fix both.

1	---
2	title: "nagara: docs"
3	summary: "The docs: what each folder holds, how files are named, and how to write a note."
4	---
5	
6	# nagara: docs
7	
8	## What each folder holds
9	
10	| Folder | Holds | Index |
11	|---|---|---|
12	| `technical-design/` | How the code works: the item lifecycle, article extraction, recipes, markdown units, the image and code describer, read-along timing, the TTS service, the item contract, persistence and storage, the common package, authentication, local development, deployment and CI, the invariants | [Technical design](technical-design/README.md) |
13	| `product-design/` | What nagara is: the ながら聞き premise, the listening experience, what gets read aloud, the queue | [Product design](product-design/README.md) |
14	
15	Which folder a note belongs in is a question about its subject, not about who wrote it. Code reading as a short placeholder rather than being read aloud is product design: it is a statement about what a listener experiences. The spoken-form derivation that produces that placeholder is technical design. The 100 ms inter-paragraph pause is product design, a number about how listening feels; folding it into the preceding timing window so there is no dead highlight zone is technical design. A note that needs both goes wherever it is mostly about and links across.
16	
17	`_templates/` holds no notes. The underscore is a sorting convention and nothing more: it floats the folder to the top of the file explorer.
18	
19	Work in flight lives in Linear, not here. A note describes something that exists; the issue that asked for it, and the open questions around it, live on the nagara project there. A note never links to an issue: the issue closes and the link rots, while the note is maintained for as long as the part exists.
20	
21	## Naming
22	
23	A note is named after the aspect it explains, in kebab-case. Not after its folder, not numbered, not dated: a date is a frontmatter field, so an index can sort on it without every filename carrying one.
24	
25	File names are unique across the whole docs folder, so a link never has to be disambiguated. Before adding a note, check the name is not taken.
26	
27	Every folder's index is called `README.md`, so that name is the one deliberate collision here: the payoff is that each index renders as a folder front page when the repository is browsed on the web. A link to a folder's index names the folder: `[the technical design](technical-design/README.md)`.
28	
29	## Frontmatter
30	
31	Every note carries `title` and `summary`, plus `created`. The summary is what shows up in search, in hover previews and in the indexes, so write it as a sentence about the subject rather than about the note.
32	
33	## How to write a note
34	
35	**A note explains how one part works.** It opens with an overview a reader can stop after, then the mechanism: the shape of the data, what calls what, in what order, with a diagram when the subject is a flow, a tree or a sequence. A reader should be able to hold that part of the system in their head without opening `api/`, `pipeline/` or `tts/app.py` first.
36	
37	`_templates/note.md` offers the sections a note can use. They are a menu, not a required shape and not a closed list: keep the ones the subject needs, add one the menu lacks when the subject asks for it, and order them so the note is easiest to follow rather than in the order the template lists them. Edge cases and failure modes go in the prose or in a callout, never in a section of their own.
38	
39	**Reasoning goes in a callout, beside the thing it justifies**, not as the spine of the note:
40	
41	```markdown
42	> [!NOTE] Why no headless browser
43	> A plain fetch handled every HTML fixture tried, including a JS-rendered Substack post: it server-renders its content. The boundary sits further out than assumed.
44	```
45	
46	A note that opens with the argument for a design makes the reader meet the case for the architecture before the architecture itself, and the argument is not what they came for. It is still worth keeping (it is what lets a decision be revisited rather than re-argued); it just is not the spine. Per-decision *why* is also the one thing the code already has, densely, at the point of each decision; what code cannot give anyone is the shape of the whole.
47	
48	Three callout kinds, and they mean different things:
49	
50	- `> [!NOTE]`: a real choice, and why it went that way.
51	- `> [!WARNING]`: a failure mode: what breaks, how it presents, and whether anything catches it. Prefer failures that have actually happened.
52	- `> [!TIP]`: an alternative considered and not taken, with the reason it was not.
53	
54	**A note is not a decision record.** There is no requirements table, no acceptance criteria, no user story, no status ladder. Those describe work being planned; a note describes something that exists.
55	
56	**A note describes the present.** No "used to", no "previously", no "no longer". An alternative that was rejected is *considered and not chosen, because…*, a standing reason, not a history of the argument.
57	
58	Create a note from `_templates/note.md`. Then **link it from at least one existing note** and add its row to its folder's index: a note nothing links to does not get read.
59	
60	## House style
61	
62	- **No hard wrapping.** One line per paragraph; let the editor wrap. Diffs then show changed sentences rather than reflowed blocks.
63	- **Explain the code, do not reprint it.** A note is not a second copy of a declaration. What each member answers goes in a table, behaviour goes in a diagram or in prose, and a snippet appears only where the code itself is the insight: an exact formula, a guard whose precise form is the point. Two to four lines when it happens. Written the other way, a note comes out a third fenced code, in a second place where nothing typechecks it and it quietly falls out of date.
64	- **Mermaid, not ASCII**, for anything with a shape. A state machine, a data model, a request's path through the system and a tree all read faster as a diagram than as a paragraph describing one, and both GitHub and Obsidian render mermaid.
65	- **Headings name their subject, and carry an emoji.** "Extraction" and "The extraction" give a reader nothing to search for; "how a URL becomes paragraphs" does. Prefer a heading that could answer a question someone typed into search. Every heading in a note opens with one emoji chosen for its subject (`## 💽 Modeling`, `### 🔑 Login`), so a reader scanning the outline sees the shape of the note before the words; the template carries the usual ones and a section you add picks its own.
66	- **Say what a thing is.** Staging a sentence against its own opposite ("it does not reject the unknown kind, it ignores it") reads as emphasis while carrying no information the plain form lacks. Write the plain form.
67	- **Prefer commas, colons and full stops to dashes.** A paragraph leaning on dashes is usually one that wants to be two sentences.
68	- **Write about our implementation.** A comparison with some other tool belongs inside a callout that justifies a decision, and nowhere else; a note is not a literature review.
69	- Close a note with a `---` rule and a `Related:` line linking the notes it actually touches.
70	
71	## Adding a folder
72	
73	A folder is three things, and they have to agree:
74	
75	1. The directory.
76	2. A `README.md` in it, carrying that folder's index.
77	3. A row in the folder table above.
78	
79	`mahou:init` will do all three and leave anything that already exists alone, or do it by hand from this list: the skills read what is here either way. What breaks is doing two of the three: a folder with no row is invisible to anyone reading this file, and a row with no folder sends people looking for something that is not there.
80

6	
7	# {{title}}
8	
9	## 🔭 Overview
10	
11	What this part is, what it is responsible for, and the main principles its design follows. Two to five sentences a reader can stop after and still know what the part does. No preamble about the note itself.
12	
13	*The sections below are a menu, not a shape. Keep the ones the subject needs, delete the rest, and add one the menu does not have whenever the subject asks for it: the menu is what has been useful so far, not a limit. Put them in whatever order makes the note easiest to follow, which is usually the thing a reader has to hold first. Every heading carries an emoji that names its subject at a glance; pick one for a section you add. Reasoning, failure modes and rejected alternatives go in callouts beside the mechanism they belong to, never in a section of their own; edge cases go in the prose or in a callout, never in a section.*
14	
15	## 🏗️ Architecture
16	
17	When the part is several components and how they interact is what needs explaining. A flowchart of the components and what crosses between them, then prose on what each component is responsible for.
18	
19	```mermaid
20	flowchart LR
21	  A[caller] --> B[the part] --> C[what it uses]
22	```
23	
24	## 💽 Modeling
25	
26	When the part stores something. An entity diagram of what the part owns, with the full field list on entities the part creates and only the relevant fields on ones that already exist, then one or two paragraphs per entity: fields, types, nullability, what each is for, who validates the shape.
27	
28	```mermaid
29	erDiagram
30	  THING ||--o{ PIECE : has
31	  THING {
32	    uuid id PK
33	    string name
34	  }
35	```
36	
37	## 📩 Flow
38	
39	When something moves through the part, or the part is triggered and does work in an order. One sequence diagram per path, numbered, high level: actors and components, no function names. Prose under it walks the numbers and covers what the diagram does not show: what happens when the input is absent, which order was chosen and what the fallback preserves.
40	
41	```mermaid
42	sequenceDiagram
43	  autonumber
44	  actor U as User
45	  participant P as The part
46	  participant S as Store
47	  U->>P: Request
48	  P->>S: Write
49	  S-->>P: Result
50	  P-->>U: Response
51	```
52	
53	## 🟢 States
54	
55	When an entity has a lifecycle. A state diagram, then what each transition requires and what each state permits.
56	
57	```mermaid
58	stateDiagram-v2
59	  [*] --> Created
60	  Created --> Ready: work done
61	  Ready --> [*]
62	```
63	
64	## ⚖️ Rules
65	
66	When a value is derived or a decision is made from an input. A flowchart of the decision, top to bottom, then the matching rules the diagram cannot carry and what each terminal outcome means for the caller.
67	
68	```mermaid
69	flowchart TD
70	  A[Input] --> B{"Usable?"}
71	  B -->|No| N((Nothing))
72	  B -->|Yes| R((Result))
73	```
74	
75	## ♠️ What it exposes
76	
77	When the part has members others call. A table of **what each member answers and who asks**, rather than a copy of its declaration. For HTTP, the endpoint, the payload shape and the response shape, with an example only where the shape is not obvious from the description.
78	
79	| Member | Answers |
80	|---|---|
81	| `something` | the question it is there to answer, and who asks |
82	
83	## ⚙️ Implementation details
84	
85	When a concrete choice a reader would otherwise get wrong matters: a configuration key, a storage format, an ordering constraint, an exact formula. Code appears only where the code is the insight, two to four lines, never a block.
86	
87	## ⏩ What is not built yet
88	
89	What is deliberately absent, and what would ask for it. Keeps the next person from reading an omission as an oversight.
90	
91	## ℹ️ Sources
92	
93	External links only, and only when one shaped the design. Other notes are linked inline where they are relevant, never collected here.
94	
95	> [!NOTE] Why it is this way and not the obvious alternative
96	> The reasoning, next to the mechanism it justifies. One callout per real choice, not a section, and not a list of every option anyone mentioned.
97	
98	> [!WARNING] The failure mode
99	> What breaks, how it presents, and whether anything catches it. Prefer failures that have actually happened.
100	
101	> [!TIP] Rejected: the alternative someone would otherwise try
102	> What it was and the constraint it failed. Worth writing only for an alternative a reasonable person would reach for; "we did not use some other vendor" is not one.
103	
104	---
105	
106	Related: [some-other-note](some-other-note.md)

6	# Technical design
7	
8	This folder holds how the code works. Each note explains one part of it; the reasoning behind a choice sits in a callout next to the mechanism it justifies. See [the docs charter](../README.md) for how a note is written.
9	
10	## Reading order
11	
12	Read these three in order since everything else depends on them:
13	
14	1. [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md): the four statuses on the item row, and the item Workflow that does all the work for one item in nine steps and restarts from the step that failed
15	2. [article-extraction](article-extraction.md): how a fetched article becomes the item's typed units, each carrying its display and spoken form
16	3. [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md): how those paragraphs get contiguous timing windows
17	
18	Then whatever you are touching.
19	
20	## What notes exist
21	
22	One row per note, kept by hand: adding a note here is part of writing it.
23	
24	| Note | Explains |
25	|---|---|
26	| [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) | The item's four statuses on its D1 row and the item Workflow that moves it through them: nine steps inside one step wrapper, with describe running one concurrent child step per description; DomainQueue's per-domain lease; the recipe runtime and the Flue author and revision agents; and a retry that restarts the Workflow from the step that failed. |
27	| [article-extraction](article-extraction.md) | How the item Workflow fetches an article and turns the recipe's markdown units into the item's typed units: a spoken form derived from each unit's display, a drop for a unit with nothing to say, and the acquisition of the article's declared images through the Images binding. |
28	| [recipes](recipes.md) | How one agent-authored script per domain extracts the domain's articles into markdown units, its versioned record, how a URL matches to it, and how agents author and revise it. |
29	| [markdown-units](markdown-units.md) | What a unit's display markdown carries for each source element, and how the shared converter and the validator turn a recipe's declared elements into it. |
30	| [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md) | The pause-fold rule that keeps per-paragraph timing windows contiguous, gapless, and exactly covering the audio. |
31	| [image-and-code-describer](image-and-code-describer.md) | Gemini through AI Gateway and its response cache: one generated sentence for a block a listener can't see, reused by the code path and the image path, floored and capped against one shared per-item budget. |
32	| [tts-service](tts-service.md) | Kokoro-82M on Modal, a separate deployable the item Workflow reaches through two web endpoints behind Modal's proxy auth: it starts a synthesis with a presigned PUT URL for the audio, then polls for the result. |
33	| [item-contract](item-contract.md) | The item routes plus /health, the item JSON, and the typed display unit whose spoken form is projected out at the response boundary. |
34	| [common-package](common-package.md) | The package both Workers build from: the shared types, the R2 key layout, presigning, the D1 schema with a query function for every read and write, the migrations generated from that schema and the cassette replay library. |
35	| [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md) | The item, recipe version and ledger rows in one D1 database both Workers share, with JSON `units` and `degradations` columns and SQL migrations generated from a schema in common/; audio and images in one R2 bucket under separate key prefixes, delivered through presigned URLs. |
36	| [authentication](authentication.md) | A single API key is the user's identity and guards every item route; audio and images reach a client as a 307 to a presigned URL, and only a backend holds the key. |
37	| [deployment-and-ci](deployment-and-ci.md) | Three deployables: the API Worker and the pipeline Worker, deployed with wrangler in a fixed order after `common/`'s D1 migrations, and the TTS service on Modal; each tree runs its own path-filtered CI checks. |
38	| [local-development](local-development.md) | Both Workers running locally on one shared state folder with D1 and R2 on disk, calling the real Firecrawl and AI Gateway and a `modal serve` copy of the TTS app, with a quick tunnel and a local proxy for Modal's audio upload. |
39	| [invariants](invariants.md) | The ten rules the code obeys, and where each one is explained. |
40	
41	## What has no note yet
42	
43	Honest gaps, so nobody assumes coverage that is not there.
44	
45	- **The read-along player.** Not yet built in `web/`, so there is no part to explain. Its mechanism facts are settled: the `requestAnimationFrame` highlight sync and the seek nudge in [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md), the shape of the surface in [the listening experience](../product-design/listening-experience.md), and the rest (memoized per-paragraph render, `transform: scale` for focus mode, the table of contents' proportional scroll) on the Read-along player milestone in Linear and the `idea/read-along-player` branch. This gap gets its note when the surface lands.

6	# Product design
7	
8	This folder holds what nagara is and what it is like to use. Each note explains one part of it; the reasoning behind a choice sits in a callout next to the mechanism it justifies. See [the docs charter](../README.md) for how a note is written.
9	
10	## What notes exist
11	
12	One row per note, kept by hand: adding a note here is part of writing it.
13	
14	| Note | Explains |
15	|---|---|
16	| [what-nagara-is](what-nagara-is.md) | A private, API-first audio read-later queue (hand it a URL, get back listenable read-along audio) built to answer one open question: does anyone besides the owner want this? |
17	| [queue](queue.md) | Every item is private to the key that created it; a voice is chosen per item or at random from a curated pool, and the status a user sees is one of queued, generating, ready, or failed. |
18	| [listening-experience](listening-experience.md) | Read-along as the product: a calm reader by default, an opt-in focus teleprompter, and navigation carried entirely by scroll and a table of contents rather than clicking into the text. |
19	| [what-gets-read-aloud](what-gets-read-aloud.md) | The article body, and nothing else: a code block and an image are each described in one spoken sentence, a table reads as prose, a link reads as its anchor text, and the author's own words are preferred wherever they exist. |
20	
21	## What has no note yet
22	
23	Honest gaps, so nobody assumes coverage that is not there.
24	
25	- **The read-along player's visual design.** [The listening experience](listening-experience.md) describes the player's shape (two reading modes, scroll-decoupled navigation), settled against a deliberately placeholder aesthetic. The design language (typography, colour, motion, brand feel) is unbuilt; it is the Read-along visual design milestone in Linear.

3	summary: "The ten constraints the code must respect, and where each one is explained."
4	created: "2026-07-29"
5	---
6	
7	# Invariants
8	
9	## 🔭 Overview
10	
11	There are ten constraints that the code must respect. Each keeps something true, and the note in each row's last column explains it.
12	
13	`CLAUDE.md` at the repo root carries the same list for agents working in the codebase. If the two disagree, this note is the explanation and that one is the summary: fix both.
14	
15	## ⚖️ Rules
16	
17	| # | Rule | Explained in |
18	|---|---|---|
19	| 1 | **One extraction is the source of truth.** The display form and the spoken form both come from one markdown segmentation of the page. The spoken form never reaches a client; the display form is never synthesized. | [article-extraction](article-extraction.md) |
20	| 2 | **Display, spoken, and timing are properties of one typed unit, never matched by text.** A dropped unit leaves the one list and takes its window with it; a length mismatch at finalize fails the item. | [article-extraction](article-extraction.md), [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) |

content.text:
**Answer:** `docs/` has two content folders, `technical-design/` and `product-design/`, plus `_templates/`. Both indexes are hand-kept tables, and every note carries `title`, `summary` and `created` frontmatter. The only top-level file beside the folder is `/home/agus/workspace/asermax/nagara/CLAUDE.md`. There is no `AGENTS.md`. I read `docs/README.md` directly and then loaded `mahou:docs`.

## Charter (`docs/README.md`, 79 lines)
- **Folders:** `technical-design/` is how the code works. `product-design/` is what nagara is. The folder is chosen by the note's subject. A note that spans both goes where it is mostly about and links across. `_templates/` holds no notes (the underscore only sorts it first). A folder needs its directory, a `README.md` index, and a row in the charter's folder table.
- **Naming:** kebab-case, named after the aspect, never the folder, a number or a date. File names are unique across all of docs. Every folder index is `README.md`.
- **Frontmatter:** `title`, `summary`, `created` (the folder indexes carry only `title` and `summary`). The summary is a sentence about the subject, not about the note.
- **Note shape:** an overview first, then sections from a menu in whatever order reads best. A note describes the present (no "used to"), is not a decision record, and has no requirements table or status ladder.
- **Callouts:** `[!NOTE]` is a real choice and why. `[!WARNING]` is a failure mode, preferably one that has happened. `[!TIP]` is an alternative considered and rejected.
- **House style:**
  - One line per paragraph, no hard wrapping.
  - Explain the code, don't reprint it (snippets are 2–4 lines).
  - Mermaid, not ASCII.
  - Every heading opens with one emoji.
  - Prefer commas and colons to dashes.
  - Write about nagara's own implementation, with comparisons only inside callouts.
  - Close with `---` and a `Related:` line.
- **Linking:** a new note must be linked from at least one existing note and get an index row.
- **Work in flight:** it lives in Linear. A note never links to an issue.
- **Index style:** hand-kept table, "adding a note here is part of writing it". Each index also has a "What has no note yet" section listing gaps.

## Template (`_templates/note.md`, 106 lines)
Frontmatter is `title`, `summary` and `created: {{date:YYYY-MM-DD}}`. Sections in the menu:
- 🔭 Overview
- 🏗️ Architecture (flowchart)
- 💽 Modeling (erDiagram)
- 📩 Flow (sequenceDiagram)
- 🟢 States (stateDiagram)
- ⚖️ Rules (flowchart TD)
- ♠️ What it exposes (member/answers table)
- ⚙️ Implementation details
- ⏩ What is not built yet
- ℹ️ Sources

It also carries the three callout examples and the closing `---` plus `Related:` line.

## Folders and notes
Lines are the file's line count. Summaries are shortened from each note's frontmatter. `docs/.obsidian/` holds editor config only.

**technical-design/** (`README.md`, 45 lines, has a "Reading order": item-lifecycle, then article-extraction, then read-along-timing)

| File | Title | Summary | Lines |
|---|---|---|---|
| `item-lifecycle.md` | Item lifecycle | Four-state machine, nine Workflow steps, DomainQueue, retry from the failed step | 367 |
| `article-extraction.md` | Article extraction | Recipe markdown units become typed units: spoken form, drop, image acquisition | 134 |
| `recipes.md` | Recipes | One agent-authored script per domain, versioned, URL matching, author and revise agents | 140 |
| `markdown-units.md` | Markdown units | What display markdown carries per source element; converter and validator | 64 |
| `read-along-timing.md` | Read-along timing | Pause-fold rule for contiguous timing windows covering the audio | 50 |
| `image-and-code-describer.md` | Image and code describer | Gemini through AI Gateway with cache; one sentence per block, shared per-item budget | 127 |
| `tts-service.md` | TTS service | Kokoro-82M on Modal, two web endpoints behind proxy auth, presigned PUT | 104 |
| `item-contract.md` | Item contract | Item routes plus /health, item JSON, typed display unit | 99 |
| `common-package.md` | The common/ package | Shared types, R2 keys, presigning, D1 schema and queries, migrations, cassette replay | 169 |
| `persistence-and-storage.md` | Persistence and storage | D1 row with JSON columns, drizzle migrations, R2 prefixes, cost ledger | 188 |
| `authentication.md` | Authentication | Single API key guards every item route; one-hour presigned R2 links | 52 |
| `deployment-and-ci.md` | Deployment and CI | Three deployables, fixed deploy order, path-filtered CI | 107 |
| `local-development.md` | Local development | Both Workers on a shared state folder, quick tunnel and local proxy for Modal | 94 |
| `invariants.md` | Invariants | The ten constraints and where each is explained | 35 |

**product-design/** (`README.md`, 25 lines)

| File | Title | Summary | Lines |
|---|---|---|---|
| `what-nagara-is.md` | What nagara is | Private, API-first audio read-later queue built to test whether anyone besides the owner wants it | 41 |
| `queue.md` | Queue | Items private to the creating key, voice per item or random, four visible statuses | 40 |
| `listening-experience.md` | Listening experience | Read-along as the product: calm reader, opt-in focus mode, navigation by scroll and table of contents | 37 |
| `what-gets-read-aloud.md` | What gets read aloud | Body only; code and images get one spoken sentence; tables read as prose; links read as anchor text | 55 |

## Invariants (`technical-design/invariants.md`)
The note is an Overview plus a table (#, rule, "Explained in") and one `[!NOTE]` callout. `CLAUDE.md` repeats the list, and the note says that if the two disagree, the note is the explanation and `CLAUDE.md` the summary.
1. One extraction is the source of truth. Display and spoken forms come from one segmentation.
2. Display, spoken and timing ride on one typed unit, never matched by text.
3. Timing windows are contiguous, and the last `end` equals the audio duration.
4. Every item route requires the key. `/health` is the only open route.
5. No Worker imports the TTS code. The item Workflow reaches it over HTTP, with no broker or sweeper.
6. Backends are chosen by configuration, never by environment name.
7. A schema change is a migration, generated by drizzle-kit and reviewed.
8. The three deployables ship separately. Only `common/` triggers other trees' checks.
9. Read-along highlight sync uses `requestAnimationFrame`, never `timeupdate`.
10. A settled recipe always runs through the deterministic runtime.

## Link hubs
Counts are the number of other notes that mention each note, so they are rough.
- **Most linked:** `item-contract` (15), `item-lifecycle` (15), `persistence-and-storage` (12), `article-extraction` (10), `common-package` (10), `invariants` (9).
- **Least linked:** `what-nagara-is` (2), `image-and-code-describer` (3), `queue` (4).
- **Indexes:** each folder README links to all of its own notes. `product-design/` and `technical-design/` link to each other (for example `listening-experience` is linked from the technical README). `invariants` links out to nine notes in its `Related:` line.

## Not yet built or planned
- **Notes with a "⏩ What is not built yet" section:** 7 of 14 technical notes (`image-and-code-describer`, `read-along-timing`, `markdown-units`, `persistence-and-storage`, `article-extraction`, `authentication`, `deployment-and-ci`), plus `tts-service`, `item-contract` and `item-lifecycle`. In product design, `what-nagara-is` ("not built yet, in order"), `what-gets-read-aloud` and `listening-experience` have one.
- **`web/` and the read-along player:** not built. The technical index lists this as a gap, and invariant 9 applies to code that does not exist yet.
- **Read-along visual design:** unbuilt, listed as a gap in the product index.
- **Smaller items:**
  - Quote voices and adjustable speed (`what-gets-read-aloud`).
  - Serving `web/` and `api/` from one origin (`deployment-and-ci`).
  - Quota enforcement and `GET /items` (`item-lifecycle`).

## Other top-level files
- `/home/agus/workspace/asermax/nagara/CLAUDE.md` holds the layout, the 10 invariants, the code style, and a "When adding something" table that routes changes to docs. It also has a `## Docs` section pointing to `docs/` and the Linear work-tracking rules. There is no `AGENTS.md`.
- `.mahou/` also exists at the repo root. I did not read it.
